questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to become a wine judge
What decides our taste and whether experts' opinions matter
The most popular crisps in the UK
Why some people are colour-blind
questions.why: They ask what taste is, why we can't agree on it, and whether it's worth listening to experts.

questions.q: What have scientists discovered about taste, according to Beth?
options: It is only a matter of personal opinion
It changes every few years
Everyone tastes food the same way
It is influenced by our genes and DNA
questions.why: Beth says scientists have discovered taste is influenced by our genes and DNA.

questions.q: When did science's understanding of how taste works begin?
options: About 25 years ago, when taste receptors were discovered
About 100 years ago, when the first taste tests were done
In ancient Greece
Only last year
questions.why: Phil says it started only 25 years ago with the discovery of taste receptors.

questions.q: Why might the same food taste sweet to one person and sour to another?
options: Because of what they ate earlier
Because some people are born with many more taste buds than others
Because of differences in the taste receptors they're born with
Because of the temperature of the food
questions.why: Beth says it's because of differences in the receptors we're born with.

questions.q: What does researcher Danielle Reed say about early genetic studies of taste?
options: They studied people from every continent and many different cultures
They were mostly about wine
They looked mainly at people of European ancestry
They proved everyone's taste is the same
questions.why: She says they 'confined ourselves to looking at a few Europeans', so understanding was limited.

questions.q: Why does Danielle mention friends who are colour-blind?
options: To argue we shouldn't criticise people's taste, since it's biology too
To explain that taste and sight are controlled by exactly the same cells
To show that colour affects taste
To say colour-blind people can't taste well
questions.why: She says we wouldn't criticise colour-blind friends, yet we feel free to criticise friends' taste.

questions.q: What does presenter Ruth Alexander ask wine judge David Kermode?
options: Which wine is the best in the world
How to become a wine judge
Whether drinking wine every day is bad for people's health in the long term
Whether wine competitions are pointless if taste is genetic
questions.why: She asks if individual, genetic taste makes the wine competition 'a pointless exercise'.

options: He agrees that the competitions are pointless but says people still enjoy them
He admits taste is personal, but judges must put their prejudices aside
He says taste is not subjective at all
He says only experts have good taste
questions.why: He says taste is subjective, but judges are encouraged, 'ordered almost, to park those prejudices'.
